analysis.one_liner: Phases lead out of paint, toys, packaging, and other consumer products and funds safe removal of lead paint from homes.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared a House subcommittee in April 1992 but the full committee never voted, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended without a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Lead poisoning was the most common environmentally caused disease among American children, and most of it came from old lead paint and lead that keeps entering the environment from products. The bill would have barred selling paint, toys, construction materials, packaging, and other goods above strict lead limits, required warning labels on lead-containing products, and funded training and certification for workers who remove lead paint safely. It cleared its House subcommittee with amendments but never received a vote from the full Energy and Commerce Committee or the House.
analysis.who_benefits: Children, who face permanent neurological damage from lead exposure, along with low-income families living in older housing with lead paint; also lead-abatement workers, who would get federally set safety training and certification standards, and nonprofit groups and universities funded to run training programs and research centers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children in older housing; lead-abatement workers

how_it_helps.text: Bans the manufacture, import, and sale of paint with more than 0.06 percent lead and toys, construction materials, inks, and other products above strict lead-content limits [S2][S3]
Phases lead out of food and product packaging, with allowable incidental lead falling to 100 parts per million after seven years [S2][S3]

Directs EPA to run a national program for detecting, monitoring, and safely abating lead-based paint, publish laboratory standards, and issue public education campaigns on lead poisoning in homes, schools, and day care centers [S2][S3]

Requires federal regulations accrediting lead-abatement training programs and certifying abatement contractors, with grants to nonprofits training the workers who do this hazardous removal work [S2][S3]

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of paint, toys, packaging, printing inks, and construction materials that use lead, and auto makers that relied on lead-based electrocoat primers for corrosion protection, who would face reformulation costs and recordkeeping, labeling, and disclosure requirements; EPA and state agencies bear the cost of administering the new programs.

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts corrosion-inhibiting coatings on motor vehicle parts with up to 1.9 percent lead and, if no substitute primer is found, allows leaded electrocoat primers on cars for another 13 to 14 years [S2][S3]

Compliance costs fall on paint, packaging, printing, and auto manufacturers, and critics argued existing law already banned lead paint in consumer products; the bill also sets up a large new EPA regulatory, labeling, and inventory-reporting apparatus [S2][S3]
Manufacturers could claim inventory information as trade-secret confidential, limiting what the public could see about who makes lead-containing products [S2][S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health payoff was large: lead is a neurotoxin with permanent effects on children, and the bill attacked both ongoing sources (products and packaging) and the legacy source (lead paint in housing). The main costs were one-time reformulation expenses for manufacturers, mostly for products like lead paint and leaded packaging that had safer alternatives already. The bill's own design conceded the auto industry's strongest case by giving leaded car primers a decade-plus escape hatch if no equivalent substitute existed.

outcome.mechanism: A House subcommittee held hearings and approved an amended version in April 1992, but the full Energy and Commerce Committee never took it up, and the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Al Swift (D-WA) introduced the bill on October 11, 1991, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee [S1][S5]
Seventeen Democratic colleagues signed on as cosponsors [S4]
The subcommittee on Transportation and Hazardous Materials held hearings in October 1991, and on April 2, 1992 approved an amended version and forwarded it to the full committee [S5]
The full Energy and Commerce Committee never held a markup, and the House never voted on the bill before the Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1][S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of lead-containing paint, packaging, and auto parts avoided new content limits, labeling rules, and disclosure requirements. Children in older housing continued to face the lead exposure the bill was designed to reduce.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 17 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill died in a Democratic-controlled committee without ever drawing a floor vote.

industries.note: The bill banned paint above 0.06 percent lead, forcing reformulation to lead-free formulas. Lead paint in older housing is the leading source of childhood lead poisoning, so the industry's cost is directly tied to the public's health gain.

It banned intentionally added lead in packaging and ratcheted allowable incidental lead down to 100 parts per million over seven years, requiring reformulation of inks, dyes, and additives. Lead from packaging enters the food and waste stream that people are exposed to.

The bill granted a long exemption for lead-based electrocoat primers on car parts (up to 1.9 percent lead) and, absent a proven substitute, allowed them for another 13 to 14 years, but eventually required a switch to lead-free primers.

industries.industry: Lead abatement contractors and training organizations
industries.note: The bill created a federally certified abatement workforce, mandatory accreditation of training programs, and grants to nonprofit trainers, locking in a credentialed industry whose work is the remedy for the lead hazard itself.
